slots.doc.title: Interview Plan
slots.role.title: Propulsion Engineer
slots.doc.thesis: Each competency has exactly one owner. If two interviewers grade the same thing, a stage is wasted, and the debrief stalls on whatever nobody owned.
slots.s1.title: Five stages, cheapest cut first
slots.s1.body: Ordered so the cheapest cut comes first. Nobody spends four hours on a thrust-stand problem to fail on something the thirty-minute screen would have surfaced.
slots.s2.title: Every competency gets one owner
slots.s2.body: Read down a column and you have one interviewer's brief. Read across a row and you have the evidence you will actually hold at debrief. The outlined cell is owned by nobody.
slots.caution.1: High-temperature materials and additive manufacturing sits on the scorecard but no stage owns it, so it will surface as unexamined doubt at debrief. Either assign it to the Tech 2 deep-dive with a written bar, or take it off the scorecard.
slots.s3.title: Questions with the bar written down
slots.s3.body: A question with no written bar is a vibe check. Each card says what a four sounds like and what a two sounds like, so two interviewers score the same answer the same way.
slots.s4.title: The debrief, and the two hard-noes
slots.s4.body: Scores are written before the room opens. The order exists to stop the most senior or the loudest voice from anchoring everyone else.
slots.gate.1: Cannot reason about a propulsion system as one coupled thermal, fluid, and structural problem. After two stages of prompting they still size a component in isolation. On a small team shipping flight hardware, that is the expensive miss.
slots.gate.2: Treats the hardware partner as an obstacle rather than a peer, and cannot name a test result that once changed their mind. Unworkable on a team this small.
slots.nongate.1: No launch-prime pedigree. No master's degree. No one specific analysis package. None of these predict propulsion judgment, and every one of them shrinks an already small pool.

loop.stages.stage.name: Recruiter screen
loop.stages.stage.job: Motivation, comp expectations, logistics. Advance fast or pass fast.

loop.stages.stage.name: Hiring manager
loop.stages.stage.job: Scope fit and ownership appetite. Sells the mission as hard as it screens.

loop.stages.stage.name: Technical screen
loop.stages.stage.job: Thermofluids and analysis against a real problem. The can-they-do-it filter.

loop.stages.stage.name: Technical deep-dive
loop.stages.stage.job: Design depth, a thrust-stand anomaly, and the numbers. Highest-signal stage.

loop.stages.stage.name: Systems & values
loop.stages.stage.job: How they work with the hardware partner when the data disagrees.

rows.label: CAD and analysis: CFD, FEA, thermal

questions.q.text: "A hot-fire reads eight percent low on thrust, but chamber pressure looks nominal. Walk me through what you rule out, in order."
questions.q.strong: Separates measurement from physics: checks load-cell calibration and stand alignment before touching the engine. Asks what changed since the last good run. Names what would disprove each theory.
questions.q.weak: Blames the injector at once and redesigns it. Trusts the thrust number without checking the stand or the sensors. Cannot say what evidence would change their mind.

questions.q.text: "Design a feed system that still delivers rated flow if one valve sticks shut. What do you cut to ship it in a week, and why is that cut safe?"
questions.q.strong: Names the failure mode first, offers two real architectures with a stated tradeoff, and says exactly what they cut under the week and why it stays safe for this failure.
questions.q.weak: Proposes one architecture with no fallback, cannot say what actually fails for the vehicle when the valve sticks, and needs the interviewer to name the tradeoff first.

questions.q.owner: HM · ownership on a small team
questions.q.text: "Tell me about a propulsion problem you owned end to end that nobody assigned you. What made it worth the effort, and what did it cost?"
questions.q.strong: A specific gap they caught before anyone flagged it, the real cost of ignoring it, the actual sequence of what they did, and who they had to convince.
questions.q.weak: Describes assigned test or analysis work as if it were initiative. No cost named, no tradeoff, no other people in the story, and no reflection.

questions.q.text: "Describe a time your analysis said the hardware was wrong and the partner disagreed. How did you settle it?"
questions.q.strong: Built test or analysis evidence before making the claim, treats the partner as competent, and reports what happened after, including where they turned out partly wrong.
questions.q.weak: The story is about being right. The hardware partner is the antagonist. No evidence step, and no sign they updated when new data arrived.

debrief.steps.step.title: Scores written and submitted first
debrief.steps.step.body: No score, no vote. Whoever has not written their scorecard does not speak first.

debrief.steps.step.title: Lowest scorer opens the room
debrief.steps.step.body: Inverts seniority on purpose, so concerns get air before the loudest enthusiasm anchors everyone.

debrief.steps.step.title: Owners read one row each
debrief.steps.step.body: Follow the heat grid. A three on a hard senior question is not a three on an easy one.

debrief.steps.step.title: Calibrate, do not average
debrief.steps.step.body: Weight for hawk-or-dove interviewers, early-round nerves, and format mismatch before comparing scores.

debrief.steps.step.title: Decide inside the hour
debrief.steps.step.body: Any single one forces extended discussion. Then hire, no-hire, or one named missing check with an owner.

handoff.consumers: 08 Recruiter Screen · 09 QA Gate · scorecard setup
handoff.assumptions: Two propulsion engineers free for the deep-dive each week. No take-home. Panel is trained on the written bars.
handoff.blocked: Owner for the high-temp materials and additive row, or removal from the scorecard
